The generalized Weierstrass semigroup at a specific point of an algebraic curve is determined by a linear coding method. This paper proposes an algorithm to calculate Weierstrass semigroups for genus 2 curves over finite fields, supported by examples.

In recent years, the development of synthesized singing voices has been revolutionized by the introduction of advanced deep learning techniques. These innovations have led to the creation of highly realistic singing voices that can be produced from a single audio sample. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the most significant breakthroughs in deep learning-based singing synthesis, focusing on the most up-to-date research from 2018 to 2020. The research focuses on the latest methods that utilize deep neural networks to generate high-quality singing voices, including the development of the SingNet model.

The comprehensive dataset of annotated birdsong recordings is crucial for developing advanced algorithms for birdsong identification and categorization. We introduce the first fully annotated dataset of 100 hours of continuous audio of birdsong recordings, featuring 12 distinct species of wild birds. This dataset is the result of a 128-hour recording period in a natural environment, utilizing a high-resolution audio recording system. We also provide a detailed description of the dataset, including its collection process, and a comparison with existing datasets.

This report outlines a method for calibrating event cameras using an advanced image reconstruction technique. By combining the benefits of both pixel-based and interpolation-based calibration methods, the neural network approach provides superior results. However, the reliance on image quality in this method can be a limitation. To address this, an event camera calibration approach based on the traditional two-point method is introduced, which relies on the inherent structure of event data.

Graph learning has been rapidly gaining attention in the field of machine learning,
due to the growing availability of graph datasets. Unlike traditional data sets,
which consist of tabular information, graph data exhibits a complex, interconnected
structure. This paper provides an in-depth exploration of graph neural networks,
including their underlying principles and applications. We begin by introducing
the concept of graph neural networks and their significance in machine learning.
We then delve into the various types of graph neural networks, discussing their
characteristics and advantages. Finally, we examine the practical applications of
graph neural networks in real-world scenarios, including social network analysis,
recommendation systems, and drug discovery.

Our study focuses on exceptional objects on derived categories of specific surface types, namely $\mathbb{P}^2$ and del Pezzo surfaces, with particular attention to weak del Pezzo surfaces possessing exactly one $(-2)$-curve. We provide a comprehensive characterization of such exceptional objects, and our findings allow us to determine their positions within the projective space $\mathbb{P}^5$ in terms of possible configurations.

A revolutionary technique known as image-guided robot-assisted surgery has the potential to revolutionize retinal procedures by offering enhanced precision and reduced invasiveness. This technology, however, is still in its early stages of development and requires further research to fully realize its benefits. In this study, we present a cutting-edge image-guided robot designed specifically for retinal procedures, which incorporates a miniature robotic system capable of precise, three-dimensional positioning. Our robot's capabilities are demonstrated through the successful execution of a precise photocoagulation treatment on a rat's retina, showcasing its potential to facilitate minimally invasive treatments. This research represents a significant milestone in the field of retinal surgery, offering a promising solution for the treatment of retinal diseases.

We define the concept of a family of polynomials, known as F-polynomials, for cluster algebras with fixed coefficients and variables, with each family having an initial value of one. We demonstrate that within the positive assignment space, the value of a F-polynomial at that space is also positive. We also prove that the initial value conjecture holds true for F-polynomials when examining cluster algebras of classification types A, B, and C, with the initial value of a F-polynomial at zero assignment being the sum of its maximum terms. Furthermore, we prove that the initial value of a F-polynomial at zero assignment is also the initial value of a F-polynomial at zero assignment for any cluster in classification C, with the initial value of a F-polynomial at zero assignment being the sum of its maximum terms.

The integration of FIDO2 and WebAuthN technologies has sparked a widespread interest in completely removing passwords from the web. However, this paper argues that while eliminating passwords is a worthy objective, it is unlikely to be achieved in the near future. The authors examine the challenges and limitations of removing passwords from the web, including the need for a seamless user experience, the cost of implementation, and the complexity of the existing web infrastructure. The paper also explores the potential benefits and drawbacks of removing passwords from the web, and provides recommendations for developers and organizations that are interested in eliminating passwords from the web. The authors believe that by understanding the pros and cons of removing passwords from the web, developers and organizations can make informed decisions about whether to adopt this technology.

In this work, we demonstrate that the conventional approach of employing a compact continuous momentum space in discrete lattice models is flawed, and propose an alternative method for the Fourier transformation of discrete lattice models.

The ubiquity of video apps in our daily lives has led to concerns about their impact on user well-being. To address these concerns, video apps often incorporate design features that encourage excessive use, such as autoplay. Our research focuses on the design of video apps, specifically the user interface's role in facilitating user engagement. We conducted a study with 18 participants, exploring their experiences with video apps, particularly the design feature of autoplay. Our findings suggest that autoplay is a key factor in user engagement, and participants expressed a desire for more control over this feature. Based on our research, we propose design guidelines to empower users and foster well-being-oriented video app design.

Reactive Turing machines, a model for reactive systems, are based on the concept of a transition function that takes the system's current state and its environment into account. This model's expressiveness is examined by considering the set of behaviors it can express, which is shown to coincide with those of deterministic systems when viewed as non-deterministic. A key characteristic behavior is defined, which is finitely executable if it can be realized by a reactive Turing machine. It is demonstrated that certain infinite behavior patterns cannot be realized by such a machine, and a method is developed to check if a behavior is executable. Additionally, a reactive Turing machine is created that can recognize non-executable behaviors.

A combinatorial Gray code is a method for generating a specific sequence of objects where each object differs from the preceding one by a minimal change.  This concept has been applied to various objects, including permutations, graphs, and more.  In this paper, we create a framework for generating Gray codes for objects that can be represented as graphs, and we apply this to create Gray codes for specific types of graphs, including those representing permutations, as well as graphs, partitions, and more.  In addition, we establish the existence of Gray codes for graphs with specific properties, including those that are planar and have specific structures.  We also examine the existence of Gray codes for other graph types, including those that are labeled and unlabeled.

The sPHENIX experiment is a fixed-target based, all-purpose detector that will be constructed within the Forward Physics Experiment Facility at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. Its primary goal is to investigate the physics of charm and beauty quarks in a fixed-target environment and probe the properties of the quark-gluon plasma created in Au+Au and U+U collisions. To achieve this, sPHENIX will leverage its capabilities in tracking, particle identification, and electromagnetic calorimetry to study the effects of the quark-gluon plasma on beauty and light charm hadrons. It will also investigate the effects of the initial state of the colliding nuclei and the influence of the jet environment on the energy loss of heavy flavor particles. To do so, sPHENIX will utilize a wide range of detectors, including a tracking system, a particle identification system, and an electromagnetic calorimeter, to measure the energy loss of beauty and charm hadrons in the quark-gluon plasma. Its design is based on the SPHENIX detector, with modifications to accommodate the fixed-target geometry and the need for a high-energy physics program. This document provides a detailed overview of the sPHENIX experiment, including its physics goals, design, and the benefits it will bring to the field of heavy ion physics.

This study introduces an innovative approach for creating meshless spatial discretization of moving domain problems. It involves a novel technique for generating spatial discretization within time-interval segments, which are inherently meshless and thus avoid issues related to domain deformation. By employing a method that ensures conforming discretization, it is possible to sidestep the complexities associated with mesh deformation. Furthermore, this approach enables the use of time-interval segments as the primary domain for simulation, which is then mapped to the actual physical domain through a bijective mapping. In conjunction with a time-discretization method based on the finite element method, this technique facilitates the solution of the underlying partial differential equations. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, it is applied to a model of a deformable beam and its performance is demonstrated through a comparison with a standard finite element method.

A circular $r$-flow on a signed graph is a mapping from the edges to the $r$-th roots of unity such that the product of these values around each vertex is unity. The circular $r$-flow number of a graph is the smallest integer r that allows for such a flow. This paper explores the circular flow properties of the join of two graphs, specifically the join of a complete graph and a subgraph, and derives upper bounds on the circular flow index of the resulting graph.

Our research focuses on the flaring activity of nearby M dwarfs, specifically stars within 20 parsecs, by analyzing data from the TESS and H-alpha telescopes. We discovered that flaring stars are characterized by intense H-alpha emissions, and our analysis of these stars revealed that they exhibit a wide range of flare durations and energies. We found that the flaring activity of these stars is influenced by their mass, with more massive stars exhibiting higher flare energies. We also found that the flaring activity of these stars is influenced by their rotation periods, and that the flaring activity of lower mass stars tends to be more intense. Our results suggest that flaring activity can be a useful tool for understanding the properties of M dwarfs, and that flaring activity can be a significant source of energy for these stars.

The emergence of hematopoietic stem cells in Drosophila melanogaster occurs concurrently with embryonic development. In the egg sac, hematopoietial cells originate from the anterior end of the embryo's interior and subsequently divide and spread throughout the embryo's body. In this research, we develop a mathematical framework to model the development of hematopoietial stem cells in the egg sac of Drosophila melanogaster. Our model utilizes a combination of partial differential equations and ordinary differential equations to describe the spatial distribution and temporal evolution of stem cells, as well as the embryo's body size. We examine the model's behavior and demonstrate its ability to replicate observed patterns of stem cell distribution and proliferation. Furthermore, we investigate the model's sensitivity to variations in key parameters and its ability to predict stem cell dynamics under different conditions.

This paper presents a novel approach to speech recognition using contrastive siamese networks. By leveraging the contrastive loss, the method identifies and associates similar speech segments, while distinguishing unrelated ones. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach can achieve accurate speech recognition without the need for extensive training.

We've developed a new scaling variable, $\xi_w$, which is crucial for understanding neutrino-nucleon scattering cross-sections in deep inelastic scattering. Our research involves using $\xi_w$ to analyze data from the MINERvA experiment, specifically focusing on neutrino and anti-neutrino interactions with carbon targets. We've compared these results to predictions from the GENIE neutrino event generator and found discrepancies, which we've attributed to differences in the quark-parton distributions used in GENIE. We've also explored how $\xi_w$ relates to the Bjorken scaling variable $x$ and have found that the choice of mass factorisation scale significantly impacts the accuracy of predictions for low $x$ values.

This research paper examines the stability of a non-linear system with an unknown parameter, employing a model-based approach to adapt to the system's dynamics. The study establishes a model of the system's behavior and uses a model-based estimator to determine the unknown parameter. A feedback control strategy is introduced to ensure the system's stability, and it is demonstrated that the resulting adaptive system exhibits regular behavior under certain conditions. Furthermore, the research shows that the system's performance converges to an optimal steady state, and it proves that the unknown parameter estimate converges to its true value. The study's findings are supported by numerical simulations.

A novel BTAI framework has been developed to model brain behavior, utilizing the hypothesis that the brain operates as an inference engine to generate actions. This framework is now expanded to accommodate the complexities of human decision-making processes, which are inherently non-stationary. A new, more comprehensive model of the human brain is presented, incorporating the capacity to adapt to changing environments. This model is tested using a decision-making task with varying reward structures, and its performance is compared to that of a standard MDP-based approach. The results demonstrate the superiority of the BTAI model, which effectively captures the dynamic nature of the task and human decision-making behavior.

We investigate the non-linear quenching of a baryon density pulse in a quark-gluon plasma, which arises from a localized source and travels along the plasma's path. The initial pulse is described by a Gaussian distribution, and the system is analyzed using a simplified model of the quark-gluon plasma, specifically the Bjorken model. The model's behavior is studied in the context of the Abelian-magnetized and Abelian-non-magnetized limits, and the results are compared to a more complex, fully non-linear model. The study reveals that the non-linear effects are minimal and that the non-linear quenching can be approximated by linear quenching with a slightly reduced effective speed of sound.

The paper investigates a specific 4-dimensional Hamiltonian system with one degree of freedom, defined by the Hamiltonian $H = \frac{1}{2}(y_1+x_1)^2 + \frac{1}{2}y_2^2 + \frac{g(x_1)}{g'(x_1)}$, which is subject to the condition $g''(x_1) > 0$. It is established that the system is non-isochronous, and its behavior is further analyzed by determining the conditions under which the system exhibits isochronous properties.

The Lorenz system, a well-known model for chaotic behavior, has been extensively researched, yet its behavior remains a subject of ongoing investigation. In this study, we examine the evolution of the Lorenz system, particularly its transition to chaos, using a novel approach based on a similarity signature curve. By analyzing the system's behavior at different parameter values, we gain insight into its similarity properties and how these properties change as the system undergoes a bifurcation. Our findings reveal that the similarity signature curve can provide valuable information about the system's behavior, including the emergence of new similarities and the system's sensitivity to parameter changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the similarity signature curve can serve as a useful tool for studying complex systems and their behavior, offering new perspectives on their structure and dynamics.

The LAN property is a fundamental characteristic of statistical models, which has been a subject of extensive research. This study focuses on LAN properties of the conditional model derived from a nonparametric semiparametric model with a nuisance infinite-dimensional parameter. Specifically, it derives the Gaussian kernels of the resulting finite-dimensional models and calculates ELT scores, which are critical for model characterization. This research also identifies ELT scores, the influence function of the ELT estimators, and the optimal influence function of finite-dimensional estimators in nonparametric semiparametric models. Furthermore, it provides a detailed analysis of model differentials and curvature, including expressions for second derivatives, which are essential for model characterization.

Building upon previous research by the first author in collaboration with H. L\"uck, we extend their theoretical framework to non-self-adjoint Laplacians on non-flat bundles over compact hyperbolic surfaces. We demonstrate Weyl's law for these types of bundles under the condition of the vanishing of the Atiyah class. Furthermore, we derive a precise formula for the spectral counting function of Laplacians on flat $U(1)$-bundles, which is expressed in terms of the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer eta invariant.

FNetAR is specifically designed to handle long-range dependencies in language modeling tasks, and it achieves this by integrating the FNet architecture with an autoregressive modeling approach. We investigate the universe's expansion history using a specific model that combines two distinct phases: a decelerating era driven by a fluid with a variable equation of state, and an accelerating era represented by a dark energy component with a constant equation of state. By applying a Bayesian analysis to SNe Ia, BAO, Hubble, and JLA data, we find that this model effectively captures the universe's expansion history, yielding a transition redshift consistent with current observations. Notably, our results suggest that the transition redshift may be influenced by the equation of state in the decelerating phase, and we also explore the possibility of a future singularity within the accelerating phase.

To address the complexities of service function chaining at the network's edge, we've developed a game-theoretic approach to optimize the service function chaining process. This approach involves a game between edge nodes, each acting as a player, to minimize the overall service delay experienced by users. By analyzing the game-theoretic equilibrium, we've found that it leads to an optimal solution, equivalent to the best possible outcome in a centralized system. This approach allows for the implementation of service function chaining in a distributed manner, as each edge node can make decisions based on its own information. Furthermore, we've proposed a distributed algorithm to help edge nodes reach the game-theoretic equilibrium, as well as a method to accelerate the convergence process. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving low service delay and efficient convergence.

In a two-dimensional disordered superconductor, a transition occurs between a thermal metal and a topological superconductor, characterized by a diffusive metal and insulating phases. This transition is marked by a distinct critical point where the system becomes a diffusive insulator, exhibiting unique transport properties. This work investigates the properties of this critical point by examining the scaling behavior of the system's conductivity and the behavior of its low-energy excitations.

The surge in popularity of social media has led to a significant increase in the number of users sharing their thoughts, feelings, and experiences, which can be used to study human behavior and emotions. However, this rise in activity has also been accompanied by a growing concern about the prevalence of depression, prompting researchers to investigate the relationship between the two. This study aims to explore the connection between depression and happiness on social media by analyzing the Twitter dataset, focusing on the co-occurrence of these emotions in tweets. By examining the frequency of tweets containing both happiness and depression, as well as those containing only one of these emotions, this research provides insights into the prevalence of these emotions and their potential link. The findings of this study have implications for understanding the impact of depression on happiness and vice versa, as well as the potential for social media to be used as a tool for monitoring mental health.

It was found that Na$_{4-\delta}$NiTeO$_6$ exhibits a magnetic structure with antiferromagnetic ordering below 10.8 K, characterized by ferromagnetic chains of Ni$^{2+}$ ions and two distinct types of magnetic ordering. The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly growing network of interconnected devices that collect and share data from their surroundings. However, the reliability of this data can be compromised due to the uncertainty inherent in multiple data sources. This uncertainty can undermine trust in IoT networks, posing a significant challenge to their functionality. To address this issue, a novel, data-driven trust assessment model is proposed in this paper. The model leverages a Bayesian network to analyze the trustworthiness of IoT devices based on their data sources. By doing so, it can accurately gauge the trustworthiness of devices in real-time, even when their data sources are subject to change. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of experiments, which reveal its ability to adapt to varying data sources and provide a reliable measure of device trustworthiness.

Cubic splines are widely used for smooth curve fitting and interpolation due to their effectiveness. However, the Gibbs phenomenon can cause unwanted oscillations in spline interpolation, particularly when approximating discontinuous functions. This issue is addressed in this study by introducing a new method for constructing a smooth cubic spline that accurately fits a set of noisy data points. This method involves minimizing a cost function that takes into account the second-order differences of the data points, and it is demonstrated to converge to the data points as the number of data points increases. Additionally, the proposed method is shown to be effective in reducing Gibbs oscillations and is applicable to both one-dimensional and two-dimensional data sets.

We investigate the properties of four-dimensional Taub-NUT spacetimes within the framework of Einstein-$\Lambda$ theory, specifically focusing on their potential to represent both black holes and cosmological models. By exploring the geometry of these spacetimes, we discover that they can be represented as either closed universes or black holes, with a specific condition on their NUT charge and cosmological constant. Furthermore, we find that certain solutions can be interpreted as wormholes, with a particular relationship between the NUT parameter and the cosmological constant. Additionally, we discuss the implications of our findings on the dynamics of these spacetimes, including the possibility of cyclic behavior and the stability of their orbits.

Accurate multimedia annotation is essential for the success of Information Retrieval applications. The current methods for automatic annotation rely on deep learning models, which are limited by their need for large, labeled datasets. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the power of unsupervised learning to enhance annotation quality. Our method involves a two-stage process, where we first use a pre-trained model to extract features from the data and then apply a clustering algorithm to group similar items together. The resulting clusters are used to generate new training data for the annotation task, which is used to train a new model that outperforms the original model. The results of our method show that it can significantly improve the accuracy of automatic multimedia annotation, even when the original dataset is limited.

A longstanding issue in ecology revolves around the capacity of large ecosystems to sustain a vast array of species, with a multitude of theories proposed to explain this phenomenon. This study presents a novel approach to understanding the capacity of large ecosystems to sustain diverse species by incorporating a concept of evolutionary development. By simulating an ecosystem where species are initially scarce, we observe how they adapt and evolve over time, with their characteristics influencing their fitness within the ecosystem. Our findings reveal that an intricate interplay between the ecosystem's structure and the species' evolutionary development is responsible for maintaining diversity within large ecosystems. Furthermore, we identify a critical threshold beyond which the ecosystem loses its ability to sustain diverse species, with this phenomenon occurring in a manner reminiscent of a phase transition.

We investigate the resilience of networks against targeted attacks, focusing on a scenario where an attacker removes nodes sequentially to minimize network connectivity. In this context, we examine the concept of an avalanche, a sequence of node removals, and its impact on network structure. Our study reveals that targeted attacks can lead to a sudden network collapse, characterized by a long sequence of avelanches, and we explore the relationship between the length of an avalanche and the time it takes for a node to be removed. Our results suggest that the distribution of avalanche lengths follows a power-law pattern, and we analyze the implications of this finding for network security.

To develop a model that can generate high-quality questions from a given text, it is crucial to incorporate the ability to perform text comprehension. This model should be able to generate questions that require the reader to apply their knowledge and skills to answer correctly. This paper introduces a new approach to question generation that involves a two-stage process. In the first stage, the model generates multiple candidate answers, and in the second stage, it selects the most suitable candidate as the final answer. This approach is based on the idea that good questions should have a range of possible answers, and the model should be able to test the reader's understanding of the text by asking questions that require the reader to select the most appropriate answer. This method is referred to as the "answer-first" approach. Experimental results show that this approach significantly improves the quality of generated questions and outperforms existing methods on multiple evaluation metrics.

A novel approach is presented for obtaining precise numerical solutions to the wave equation in two-dimensional space with a specific boundary condition. A method is developed to mitigate the effects of a standard artificial absorption technique, known as perfectly matched layers (PML), which is often used in such problems. A novel approach is developed to approximate the wave equation in a manner that eliminates the need for the PML to handle the problem. This method is based on the concept of extending the wave equation to a higher-dimensional space and then projecting it back to the original space. This method is shown to be effective in achieving exponential convergence rates for the PML error. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the efficacy of this new approach.

The study of droplet arrays' fluid dynamics is explored, focusing on the influence of droplet size, inter-droplet distance, and substrate properties on their collective behavior. This investigation utilizes a computational model to analyze how the arrangement of droplets affects their fluid dynamics, which is then validated by experiments involving the manipulation of droplet size and substrate characteristics. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of droplet array responses, which can be applied to various fields, including microfluidics and bio-inspired engineering.

The Internet of Things (IoT) has become an integral part of our daily lives, with numerous applications that require stringent Quality of Service (QoS) standards. To meet these demands, a new network architecture is being developed, incorporating a centralized controller to oversee the allocation of network resources. This paper introduces a resource allocation strategy for the IoT network, focusing on the efficient utilization of radio spectrum resources. The proposed approach employs a centralized controller to assign radio resources to IoT devices, with the aim of minimizing the total energy consumption of the network. The results of a comprehensive simulation study demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method in optimizing energy consumption.

We propose a novel approach for determining distances between symmetric positive definite matrices, drawing upon principles of Riemannian geometry. Our method employs a vector-valued distance, which can be tailored to various applications by selecting an appropriate weighting matrix. To facilitate practical implementation, we develop an algorithm for calculating this distance and demonstrate its convergence. Notably, this approach can be applied to solve a range of optimization problems, including those involving low-rank matrix approximation, which we exemplify through two specific cases.

The integration of a hydrogen network into a power system can help mitigate the variability of renewable energy sources by utilizing excess energy during periods of surplus and storing it for later use. This integration can be achieved by leveraging existing hydrogen networks, which can be utilized for power system balancing. This paper proposes an approach to integrate a hydrogen network into an energy system with variable renewable energy sources, and presents a simulation of the system's operation. The simulation results show that the hydrogen network can provide significant system services, particularly during periods of high renewable energy production, and highlights the potential for hydrogen networks to contribute to system balancing.

We've developed a method to determine subsurface horizontal magnetic fields using travel time measurements, which can be obtained from helioseismic observations. By analyzing the anisotropy in travel times, we can estimate the orientation of these fields, which is crucial for understanding solar phenomena. Our approach is based on a model that relates travel time anisotropy to the orientation of magnetic fields, which can be validated through simulations. We've also shown that our method can be used to estimate the inclination of magnetic fields, which is important for understanding solar activity. Our method has been tested using simulated data, which shows that it can accurately estimate the orientation of magnetic fields, even in the presence of noise.

The generation of squeezed light is a pivotal development in quantum technology, enabling breakthroughs in quantum sensing and information processing. Our research utilizes a novel technique involving the combination of a high-quality optical cavity and a non-linear waveguide to create a system that can produce highly efficient squeezed light. By leveraging the unique properties of the waveguide, we are able to achieve efficient coupling of the cavity to the waveguide, thereby facilitating the generation of squeezed light with high power. Our results demonstrate the potential of this approach in creating high-quality squeezed light sources for a variety of quantum applications.

This research focuses on determining the optimal control strategy for a drone to reach its target location as quickly as possible, given that it can apply control forces within a specified range. By applying Pontryagin's Minimum Principle, we derive the minimum energy required to move the drone between any two points, and we also calculate the maximum possible speed at which the drone can achieve this. Furthermore, we obtain the time interval during which the drone can apply control forces, and we develop an algorithm to find the control strategy that minimizes the time taken to reach the target. Additionally, we prove that this control strategy is the only one that can guarantee the drone reaches its target location in the minimum time. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we provide numerical examples and simulations.

In 1984, Kosaraju and Uzan introduced the concept of additive codes over finite fields. This concept has been further developed by various researchers, including H\"ammerich and Ulufinkula, who defined additive conjugacy codes. This study focuses on characterizing specific types of additive conjugacy codes - those corresponding to linear cyclic codes and semilinear cyclic codes. Additionally, we examine how these codes relate to linear and semilinear cyclic codes through the use of MacWilliams identities.

The 2020 survey by the American Physical Society's Division of Nuclear Physics revealed a significant disparity in the representation of physicists from minority groups in the survey's data. A closer examination of the data indicates that minority physicists are more likely to work at the College Board's lowest-paid institutions, such as predominantly undergraduate institutions and community colleges. This correlation raises concerns about the challenges minority physicists face in the job market, prompting the need for additional support and resources.

This research examines the polarization of W bosons produced in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, specifically in the dielectron and di-muon decay channels. The analysis utilizes a dataset collected by the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider in 2016, with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$. The study focuses on the production of W bosons in association with two or more jets, utilizing the angular distribution of lepton-jet pairs to determine the polarization fractions. The findings show that the fractions of transverse, left-handed, and right-handed polarization are 0.45, 0.27, and 0.28, respectively. The results are consistent with the predictions of the Standard Model.

The study of $B\to D\ell\nu_l$ decays is crucial for understanding the form factors of $B\to D$ transitions and the $|V_{cb}|$ CKM matrix element. This research focuses on the semileptonic decay $B\to D\ell\nu_l$ within the framework of light-conet QCD factorization, incorporating the twist-2 and twist-3 distribution amplitudes of the $D$-meson. By deriving the necessary distribution amplitudes from lattice QCD data, we calculate the form factors of $B\to D$ transitions and compare them to the results from QCD sum rules and lattice QCD.

We investigate the eigenvalues generated by the power hypergraph, which is derived from the power graph of a finite group. Our analysis focuses on the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix of this power hypergraph, which are found to be an essential component of the overall spectrum. We establish that the eigenvalues of the power hypergraph can be directly correlated to those of the power subgraphs, thereby enabling us to draw on established results from graph theory. We also demonstrate that the hypergraph is primitive and we derive upper and lower bounds for its largest eigenvalue.

Research on mega-constellations, such as Starlink and OneWeb, has been ongoing for some time, with a focus on their ground-based effects. One area of study is the localisation capabilities of these constellations, with a view to repurposing them for cooperative localisation on Earth. This paper investigates the localisation performance of a small number of satellites working together to determine their positions relative to each other and those of ground receivers. It employs a Bayesian approach to estimate the satellite positions and compares this method to least squares estimation. The results, derived from simulations, demonstrate the localisation capabilities of these constellations, with Starlink showing improved accuracy as the number of satellites increases, while OneStar demonstrates better localisation when the number of receivers is increased.

The 2011 detection of transit timing variation (TTV) in the hot Jupiter HD 80606 b revealed its significant orbital migration since discovery. This study presents a new, precise ephemeris for HD 80606 b, derived from a combination of high-precision transit timing measurements and long-term photometric monitoring. The new ephemeris, with a precision of 1.7 minutes, is consistent with previous measurements and shows no evidence of TTV, indicating that the star's outer companion has not influenced the hot Jupiter's orbit in the past decade. This ephemeris can be used to optimize future observation schedules for HD 209335b, a similar hot Jupiter, to maximize the detection of TTV, which could provide insights into its orbital migration and the influence of its outer companion on the system's dynamics.

The calibration of signals is a critical step in uncovering the secrets of the cosmos, and researchers have been striving to enhance its sensitivity and accuracy. Recent advancements in signal processing have led to the development of novel methods, such as employing multiple reference sources, applying statistical techniques, and utilizing machine learning algorithms. This study introduces an innovative technique for calibrating signals from point-like sources, drawing inspiration from the concept of 'blind source separation'. This method, known as 'blind reconstruction', involves identifying and removing distortions from the signal without prior knowledge of the distortions themselves. It achieves this by utilizing a set of calibration-free signals, and can be applied to a wide range of observational data, including those from radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray telescopes. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to a simulated dataset, and its potential to improve the accuracy of calibration is highlighted.
We prove that for algebraic GKM manifolds and their equivariant vector bundles, if two such bundles have identical equivariant Chern classes, then they are equivalent to each other.
We establish a refined form of the prime number theorem for a specific class of L-functions, characterized by the absence of zeros in the right half-plane.

In clinical trials, the analysis of mixed models with repeated measures is a common practice. These models are often used to analyze categorical time variables, but doing so can result in a loss of information and lead to biased estimates. A new approach to this problem is proposed, utilizing a piecewise linear model that preserves the information in time, accounts for nonlinearity, and incorporates a penalty to prevent overfitting. This method is demonstrated through simulations and a real-world example, showcasing its effectiveness in handling categorical time and its ability to provide accurate results.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking crowdsourcing algorithm for routing connected vehicles, leveraging the power of crowdsourced data to optimize traffic flow. The proposed method, known as the Crowdsourced Information-aided Proximal Policy Optimization (CIPPO) algorithm, utilizes real-time traffic information gathered from vehicles to inform routing decisions. Theoretical analysis confirms CIPPO's convergence to an optimal policy, and its performance is validated through simulations using real-world traffic data from the SUMO simulator. The results demonstrate that CIPPO outperforms existing routing algorithms, such as the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm, in terms of average travel time and network throughput. Furthermore, a theoretical lower bound on average travel time is established, and CIPPO's performance is shown to approach this optimal limit. The study also examines the impact of various factors on CIPPO's performance, including the accuracy of crowdsourced traffic information, the number of vehicles reporting traffic data, and the number of vehicles being routed. The results indicate that CIPPO's performance improves with more accurate and abundant traffic information, and that it can effectively handle complex traffic scenarios with a large number of vehicles.

Recent studies have shown that certain neural network training algorithms tend to settle into local minima with flat landscapes, leading to improved generalization performance. However, little is known about the characteristics of these flat-minima regions. To address this, we developed a new approach to identify and analyze the flat-minima regions in a neural network's loss surface. By applying our method to various neural network architectures and training algorithms, we discovered that flat-minima regions are typically characterized by a unique structure in the neural network's weight matrix. Furthermore, we found that the flat-minima regions are closely related to the neural network's capacity to fit the training data, and that the flat-minima regions are more likely to occur when the neural network is over-parameterized. These findings provide new insights into the nature of flat-minima regions and their role in neural network training.

A novel approach to suppressing electromagnetic interference in wireless radio systems employs a frequency-selective limiter based on reflective diodes. This innovative design incorporates a bandpass filter to target specific interfering frequencies, thereby preserving desired signals. Theoretical analysis and simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the limiter in attenuating unwanted signals by up to 20 dB, while allowing desired signals to pass unimpeded. Furthermore, the proposed design is scalable, enabling the integration of multiple reflective diodes to enhance its performance.

This study introduces a novel SIR model that integrates the dynamics of infectious diseases and the economic impact of controlling them. The model's behavior is analyzed through the lens of the fundamental reproduction number, which is derived from the basic matrix. The model's solutions are studied in terms of their stability and persistence over time. The model's parameters are estimated using a dataset from the COVID-19 pandemic in Italy. The model's behavior is explored through simulations that demonstrate the effect of various control measures on the spread of the disease.

We suggest using a technique to generate numerical representations of words and phrases by relying on the relationships between words in sentences. Our approach, which is based on a technique called skip-gram, uses a type of artificial neural network that learns from sentence structures. Our experiments show that the numerical representations generated using our approach outperform existing methods in tasks such as identifying word synonyms and phrases.

In the context of random geometric graphs, we investigate the $k$-th order components, which are defined as the maximal subgraphs with a specific property. We derive precise estimates for the mean and variance of the number of $k$-th order components, showing that these estimates are directly proportional to $n^{k+1}$ and $n^{k+2}$, respectively, as the number of vertices $n$ approaches infinity.

A novel approach to studying rotating stars' equilibrium structures is developed by employing a Lagrangian framework that incorporates the effects of rotation. This formulation is derived from the fundamental principles of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics, and it's used to derive the linear perturbation equations for fully rotating stars. These equations are then analyzed in the context of the adiabatic approximation, and the resulting eigenvalue problem is used to assess the stability of rotating stars' equilibrium states.

This research introduces a novel approach to predicting web user visits by leveraging the concept of visit intention, focusing on the specific case where users have a clear, pre-planned intent to revisit a website. To achieve this, we developed a machine learning model that utilizes user behavior patterns, including past browsing history, to predict future visits. The effectiveness of our approach was evaluated using a dataset of actual user web interactions, demonstrating its ability to accurately forecast user intentions.

A reconfigurable intelligent surface, referred to as RIS, is an emerging technology that can be used to create favorable communication paths by dynamically adjusting the signal's phase and amplitude. A new transmissive RIS, referred to as TRIS, is proposed in this study, which is capable of reconfiguring the communication environment to enhance the wireless network's performance. A TRIS prototype was developed and tested in a real-world setting, and its performance was analyzed in terms of the received signal's quality. The results showed that the TRIS can effectively improve the signal quality in poor communication conditions. The study also examined the impact of the TRIS's size on the strength of the signal it can produce, and it was found that a larger TRIS can produce a stronger signal. Furthermore, a theoretical model was developed to predict the strength of the signal produced by the TRIS, and this model was validated by comparing its predictions to the experimental results. The model was also used to calculate the optimal placement of the TRIS in a given environment, and it was found that this placement can significantly improve the signal quality.

Offline reinforcement learning, which involves training from a static dataset, has garnered significant attention in recent years. The primary challenge in offline RL is striking a balance between data efficiency and safety, with agents needing to make the most of limited data while avoiding unsafe states. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method called DRPO, which combines data-driven exploration and policy optimization. By integrating an entropy-based objective function, DRPO encourages the exploration of new states while maintaining safety through a risk-sensitive constraint. The experimental results demonstrate DRPO's superiority over existing state-of-the-art offline RL methods across multiple Atari games.

In this study, we demonstrate that polymorphic functions adhere to constraints imposed by their type signatures, known as type-inference properties. The research builds upon earlier work by Richard Bird and Philip Wadler, expanding their findings to encompass more complex types. The research, conducted in the context of System F, an extension of the simply typed lambda calculus, leverages a novel proof technique grounded in logical deduction. The proof process commences by establishing a logical equivalence between the terms of System F and a graph-based representation. The analysis then proceeds to examine the behavior of polymorphic functions within this representation, ultimately deriving the type-inference properties. The research culminates in a detailed proof of the properties for all types, showcasing the effectiveness of the adopted method.

The analysis of the galaxy's spectrum reveals a redshift of $z=2.163$, with a recession velocity of $10,500$ km/s. Furthermore, we have determined the galaxy's physical properties, including its stellar mass, star formation rate, and dust content. The results indicate that the galaxy has a stellar mass of $1.1 \times 10^{11}$ solar masses, a star formation rate of $115$ solar masses per year, and a dust content of $1,100$ solar masses. The galaxy's star formation rate is consistent with its stellar mass, suggesting that it is a typical galaxy at $z=2.163$. In the context of the three-body problem, we examine configurations where a specific combination of collisions occurs, known as generalised syzygies. We develop an analytical method to calculate the precise timing of these configurations, and subsequently, we derive an algorithm to numerically identify such collision sequences.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) is a more advanced technique than conventional fluorescence imaging due to its ability to provide detailed information about the molecular and cellular composition of cells. However, the conventional time-domain analysis method used in FLIM is computationally intensive and time-consuming. To address this issue, we have developed a new method for estimating the fluorescence lifetime of a single exponential using a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained on simulated data. This DNN-based approach is capable of accurately estimating the fluorescence lifetime of a single exponential, even when the data is noisy. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the DNN-based method can be used to estimate the average fluorescence lifetime of a region of interest in a FLIM image, and that the accuracy of the estimates is comparable to that of a conventional algorithm.

In recent years, personalized product search has become a key focus in recommendation systems. A common approach to modeling user preferences is to use a sequence of user interactions, but this method often overlooks the impact of contextual factors such as location and time. To address this limitation, we propose a new model that integrates contextual information into user preference modeling. By employing a multi-modal approach, we capture the context of user interactions and combine it with user behavior data to improve the accuracy of product ranking. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in surpassing existing methods.

Graph embedding is a crucial technique in data analysis that involves transforming graph data into a lower-dimensional space. However, the stability of these embeddings can be compromised by the inherent complexity of the data. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the concept of stability in statistical learning theory. By employing a regularization method that incorporates the Lipschitz property, we enhance the robustness of the embeddings. To this end, we propose a novel framework that integrates the Lipschitz regularization into the graph convolutional autoencoder, which is then applied to various graph datasets. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in improving the stability of the embeddings.

In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access is particularly beneficial due to its reduced signaling overhead. However, the effectiveness of grant-free access is hindered by the presence of multiple users transmitting simultaneously, leading to severe interference. To address this challenge, we propose a novel grant-free multiple access technique that combines the advantages of code-division multiple access and non-orthogonal multiple access. Our approach involves the use of a joint optimization framework to allocate power and user association, thereby minimizing the probability of missed detection. To address the non-convex nature of this optimization problem, we develop an efficient iterative algorithm that can be applied to both uplink and downlink scenarios. Our simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in improving the performance of massive machine-type communications.

A novel method for compressed sensing is introduced, which utilizes a sparse coding matrix that is highly effective in representing a given signal. This approach, referred to as learned compressed sensing, involves training the coding matrix to minimize reconstruction errors, thereby enhancing measurement efficiency. We propose a new matrix architecture that enables the learned compressed sensing method to achieve optimal performance. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over traditional methods, including orthogonal measurements and dictionary-based reconstruction.

Recent advancements in deep neural networks have led to significant improvements in various applications, including computer vision and natural language processing. However, the performance of these models is often hindered by the lack of data and the presence of domain shifts. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach that leverages random data augmentation to enhance the performance of deep neural networks in domain adaptation and generalization tasks. By applying this technique, we demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the accuracy of models trained on small datasets and tested on unseen domains. Our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in a range of applications, including image classification, text classification, and image retrieval.

This paper proves that for any finite-dimensional complex Jordan algebra A, the algebra 2-local inner derivations DA are equivalent to its derivations Der(A). The same conclusion also applies to the special case where A consists of self-adjoint matrices over a finite field.

Berry's phase is a geometric property that can be acquired during adiabatic changes in a system's parameters. This phase is typically associated with the ground state of the system, but it can also be induced in excited states under specific conditions. This study focuses on the behavior of Berry's phase in relation to the energy levels of a two-dimensional harmonic oscillator, particularly in adiabatic transformations of the oscillator's frequency. It is demonstrated that the Berry's phase can be obtained not only in the ground state, but also in the first excited state under these specific conditions. Furthermore, the research explores the behavior of Berry's phase in adiabatic changes of the oscillator's shape, and it is found that the phase can be obtained in the first excited state when the oscillator's shape changes. This study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the behavior of Berry's phase in excited states and may have implications for the development of quantum technologies.

The investigation of compacton matter waves in a binary mixture of two Bose-Einstein condensates is carried out using the relativistic mean-field theory. The compacton ground state is examined in detail, along with the stability of small-amplitude oscillations. The conditions necessary for the existence of compacton matter waves are also explored, and it is found that their stability depends on the balance between the relativistic effects and the attractive relativistic mean-field interaction. The stability of these waves is found to be influenced by the compacton matter wave's amplitude, with the relativistic effects playing a significant role in determining their stability.

This paper establishes a method for approximating any continuous function with a
diffeomorphism, and demonstrates that in certain function spaces, a continuous
function can be closely approximated by a smooth function with a specific property.
Furthermore, it is shown that any compact set can be closely approximated by a
smooth, convex, and star-shaped object. These findings are relevant to a problem
posed by the mathematician L. V. Kantorovich in relation to the Wasserstein metric.

We've developed a novel approach to axion physics, incorporating axion-like particles into a lattice simulation framework. This involves axions interacting with Standard Model gauge fields through an anomaly-driven coupling. To validate our concept, we've created a lattice model that mimics the interaction between axions and Standard Model gauge bosons. This model can be integrated into existing lattice simulations, paving the way for the exploration of axion physics in a non-perturbative framework.

This research introduces an innovative approach to enhance the performance of standard processors through collaborative hardware-software techniques. By integrating these elements, processors can efficiently utilize their capabilities to accelerate specific tasks, particularly those requiring high-performance hardware accelerators. The proposed framework, named \textit{AutoFlow}, enables processors to automatically identify suitable hardware accelerators and execute tasks using the most suitable software/hardware combinations. The effectiveness of \textit{AutoFlow} is demonstrated through its application to a range of tasks, including convolutional neural networks, matrix multiplication, and image compression. The results show that \textit{AutoFlow} significantly outperforms traditional hardware-software co-design methods, achieving notable improvements in performance and energy efficiency.

Deep networks trained on vast image databases have greatly improved the performance of computer vision tasks. However, these models are often too complex to be used in real-time applications, such as those in robotics. This paper presents a new method for reducing the size of neural networks by training a smaller, simplified version of the network that can be deployed on embedded systems. This approach uses a combination of neural architecture search and pruning to find the most efficient network structure, which is then used to guide the training of a smaller, more efficient network. This method is applied to a network that detects objects in images, and the results show that it can achieve similar performance to the original network while being significantly smaller and faster to run on embedded systems.

The existence of regular solutions to a quasi-linear elliptic system with pointwise and high-order singularities is proven using the regularity of degenerate elliptic equations' solutions. This involves applying fixed point theory and changing variables to transform the system with high-order singularities into one with pointwise singularities. Ultimately, solutions are shown to be in C^{1,\alpha} for any α in the range 0 < α < 1.

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been extensively used in various applications, particularly in tasks requiring long-term dependencies. However, their training is often hindered by the vanishing gradient problem, which hinders the learning of long-term dependencies. To address this issue, researchers have introduced various techniques, including LSTMs, GRUs, and attention mechanisms. Despite these advancements, the effectiveness of RNNs in learning long-term dependencies remains a challenge. To tackle this problem, we propose a new approach called the Adaptive Learning Rate Recurrent Neural Network (ALRNN). This method dynamically adjusts the learning rate during training, which significantly enhances the model's ability to learn long-term dependencies. By comparing ALRNN with traditional RNNs, we demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing approaches in various tasks, including sentiment analysis and sequence prediction.

In Markov Decision Processes, we've developed an algorithm for learning a policy that maximizes the average reward per time step. The key to this is proving the existence of a stable state where the expected reward is consistent, along with a corresponding value function that represents the expected total reward from any given state. Our approach relies on a novel method of learning, where we first determine the best action in each state, then use this information to guide our learning process, ensuring that we converge to the optimal policy. The algorithm's performance is characterized by a specific rate of convergence, which depends on the complexity of the Markov decision process and the desired level of accuracy.

Our research focuses on producing extremely intense, attosecond electron bunches with high polarization levels through the interaction of a specially designed, partially reflective laser with a plasma wakefield accelerator. This approach leverages the plasma wakefield to generate electrons with high energy and a unique polarization pattern, which is then amplified by the laser's circular polarization. By carefully controlling the interaction between the laser and the accelerating field, we can achieve an unprecedented level of electron brightness and polarization, which is crucial for applications in advanced electron accelerators. Furthermore, our method allows for the creation of electron bunches with a specific polarization orientation, which is highly desirable for applications in electron free-electron lasers and other cutting-edge technologies.

This primary field, which is a consequence of the Higgs field's breaking, dictates the direction of the universe's evolution, and is responsible for the emergence of life. The 'vital force' is a manifestation of this field, and is a result of its interaction with the Higgs field, which dictates the direction of the universe's evolution. The availability of open research findings is essential for developing policies grounded in scientific evidence, particularly in Science, Technology, and Innovation fields.  Despite the importance of open access, a comprehensive understanding of the barriers to accessing and utilizing research outcomes is lacking.  This study examines the obstacles to accessing and utilizing research outcomes from the perspectives of researchers and policymakers in the Philippines, a developing country with a limited access to research outcomes.  This research is based on a survey of 100 researchers and policymakers in the Philippines, a country with a limited access to research outcomes.  The results of the study reveal that the barriers to accessing and utilizing research outcomes are primarily due to financial constraints, inadequate research infrastructure, and a lack of policy support.  The study also highlights the need for increased collaboration between academia and industry to improve the accessibility and usability of research outcomes.  The findings of this study have important implications for the design of policies aimed at improving the accessibility and usability of research outcomes in the Philippines, a country with a limited access to research outcomes.

The growing adoption of smartphones has led to an alarming increase in side-channel vulnerabilities, rendering devices susceptible to unauthorized access. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods to detect side-channel attacks, but these approaches are often hindered by the need for specialized datasets and expertise. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel, automated method for detecting side-channel attacks using audio data. By utilizing a unique audio processing technique, we can extract relevant information from the device's recordings, and then employ a machine learning algorithm to accurately classify side-channel attacks. Our approach has been tested on a large dataset of recordings, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying various types of attacks, including passcode entry, voice commands, and audio playback. Furthermore, we have analyzed the performance of our method under different conditions, including variations in recording quality and device models. Our findings suggest that this approach has the potential to be a powerful tool for protecting against side-channel attacks, and we have made the necessary code and data publicly available to facilitate further research and development.

The Ethereum blockchain has become a decentralized platform for various applications, including financial markets, by enabling the execution of smart contracts. To better understand the dynamics of the Ethereum network, we analyze its structure and properties, focusing on account relationships and interactions. By applying network analysis, we identify distinct account types and their connections, revealing significant differences in their transaction patterns. Our analysis also examines how network structure influences account value, revealing that certain accounts are disproportionately valuable compared to others. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of network structure on account value over time, revealing that its influence has diminished in recent years.

We investigated how the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface responds to light by analyzing its electrical properties under various conditions. We found that the interface's resistance increases when exposed to light, but this effect is amplified when the sample is cooled down. This phenomenon is consistent with the idea that light causes the creation of electron-hole pairs that scatter electrons, thereby reducing the number of electrons available for conduction. We also observed that the increase in resistance is more pronounced at low temperatures, suggesting that light-induced scattering is particularly effective in this regime. Furthermore, our results indicate that the magnitude of this scattering effect depends on the properties of the light source, such as its energy and intensity. Overall, our findings provide new insights into the electronic properties of the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ interface and open up new avenues for the study of light-induced changes in this system.

The study of provability within the BV logic is found to be decidable with a complexity of NEXP-complete. A systematic approach to the proof process is presented, allowing for a detailed examination of the syntactic characteristics of provable formulas in this logic.

We establish the pentagon identity for the quantum dilogarithm function proposed by Frenkel and Turaev, as well as the hexagon identities for the boundary quantum dilogarithm, which was suggested by Gukov and Li.

We've developed a new, deep learning-based approach to estimating photometric redshifts using a combination of galaxy properties and spectroscopic data. This method is trained on a large dataset of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and uses a graph neural network to account for the complex relationships between different galaxy properties. Our model outperforms existing methods in predicting redshifts for a large sample of galaxies, and we've found that it can accurately estimate redshifts for a wide range of galaxy types. We've also found that our model is robust to variations in the training dataset, and we've successfully applied it to a large sample of galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Our results suggest that this method has the potential to significantly improve redshift estimates for a wide range of astronomical studies.

Complex computer models can be approximated using Gaussian Process emulators, which are often difficult to fit due to computational constraints. To address this issue, a novel method has been developed for Bayesian inference in these models, utilizing a two-stage approach. Initially, a basic model is fitted to the data, and then the parameters of this model are re-estimated using a pre-computed lookup table. Subsequently, the parameters of this table are estimated using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. This approach is demonstrated through its application to a 10-dimensional model of a 3D convection problem, which features multiple computational domains.

We have developed an exact quantization approach for the QC-DMRG method, enabling its application to two-electron systems with a guaranteed accuracy. The resulting method, denoted as QC-DMRG, employs a specific basis set and a particular Hamiltonian representation to achieve optimal results. The analysis of the optimal bond dimension for this method reveals that it is exactly equal to 2, and our calculations show that the ground state energy of two-electron systems can be determined with a high degree of accuracy using this approach. The findings of this study have implications for the development of quantum algorithms for simulating molecular systems, and may contribute to the development of more accurate quantum chemistry methods.

We explore a non-standard muon anomalous magnetic moment, examining the
possibility of a non-Abelian gauge symmetry, $SU(2)_X$, being extended to the
Standard Model. This allows for a novel interaction between the muon and the W boson,

We introduce a freely accessible end-to-end data analysis pipeline for CMB experiments, called CosmoPipeline, which is designed to handle the full data processing workflow from raw data to cosmological parameter estimation. This includes a comprehensive suite of data processing tools, such as data extraction, noise assessment, and map generation, as well as a cosmological parameter estimation module. By incorporating a novel model-based noise estimation technique, CosmoPipeline can accurately estimate noise levels in both time-domain and map data, which is crucial for accurate cosmological parameter estimation. We have successfully tested CosmoPipeline with data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope and found that it produces results consistent with previous analyses, while also providing a more accurate and detailed cosmological parameter estimation. We envision CosmoPipeline to be a valuable tool for future CMB experiments, which will require the ability to handle large datasets and perform complex analyses in a timely and efficient manner.

We investigate the Turing instability in a nonlinear reaction-diffusion system, which is characterized by two interacting components, and we explore the effects of a nonlocal reaction term on the system's behavior. By examining the system's stability through linear analysis, we derive the conditions necessary for Turing instability to occur, and we validate our findings through numerical simulations that reveal the system's pattern formation.

A specific modification of pure Yang-Mills theory is investigated, incorporating a 'phantom field' with a unique characteristic. This field has a kinetic term with a negative sign and is coupled to the Yang-Mills theory through a Lagrangian. This theoretical framework is notable for its ability to eliminate quantum corrections at the deformation's zeroth order, due to the presence of the phantom field. Additionally, the theory is free from non-perturbative instabilities, as it cannot be spontaneously broken by the negative kinetic term. Furthermore, the theory exhibits a unique property where the loop expansion is absent, as all quantum corrections are cancelled out. This theoretical framework is also capable of being coupled to other fields, as it can be shown that the quantum corrections are also cancelled out when coupled to a scalar field. This theoretical framework is further explored by examining the potential to couple the theory to gravity.

The polarization characteristics of photoluminescence from GaAs/AlGaAs nanowires were examined using a comprehensive theoretical approach. A quantum wire model incorporating the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism was utilized to calculate the polarization properties. The findings revealed that the degree of polarization is heavily influenced by the applied electric field, with a notable increase in polarization occurring when the electric field surpasses a specific threshold. The observed polarization behavior was also found to be highly sensitive to the geometric properties of the nanowire, with variations in diameter and barrier width having a substantial impact on the polarization characteristics. The study provides valuable insights into the polarization properties of nanowires, which may have significant implications for their use in optoelectronic devices.

To successfully negotiate a deal, it's crucial to understand the opposing side's priorities and goals. This research focuses on developing an approach to infer an opponent's priorities from their proposals during negotiations. By integrating machine learning with game theory, the method can accurately predict the opponent's goals and inform strategic decision-making. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in accurately estimating the opponent's goals and outperforming traditional methods.

In braneworld models where dynamical string tension is a possibility, strings and matter may not be confined due to the universe's expansion. We explore brane dynamics in models where D-branes coexist with a background anti-D-brane, and our findings indicate that the effective string tension decreases as the universe evolves.

In field experiments conducted in real-time, researchers often need to account for multiple characteristics of the subjects or locations being studied to ensure accurate results.  A key challenge in online settings is that researchers must make decisions quickly and without the ability to examine all available data beforehand.  A new approach to tackling this issue is presented, which involves using a dynamic model to balance the multiple characteristics of the subjects or locations being studied.  This method, which is based on the concept of stochastic approximation, allows researchers to make decisions that balance the multiple characteristics of the subjects or locations being studied in real-time.  This approach is demonstrated to be effective in both theory and practice, and its benefits are illustrated through a case study of a real-time experiment conducted by a major online retailer.

A detailed analysis of the (001)-Si/(001)-gamma-Al2O3 interface has been conducted using advanced computational methods. By applying density functional theory, researchers have identified the atomic and electronic properties of the interface, including the interface orientation, atomic structure, and electronic properties. The study found that all silicon atoms at the interface are coordinated with four oxygen atoms, resulting in a stable and well-ordered interface. The analysis also revealed that the interface is characterized by a specific electronic structure, consisting of a band gap and a specific density of states. The study's findings provide valuable insights into the nature of the interface and its electronic properties, which may have important implications for the development of novel semiconductor devices.

In four-dimensional axion-dilaton system, we employ machine learning techniques to estimate functions related to Black Hole physics, utilizing exact solutions obtained through numerical relativity. Our approach involves training neural networks to predict functions, with our chosen method achieving exceptional accuracy. We also investigate the utility of machine learning in solving Einstein's equations, with a focus on constructing multi-black hole solutions.

A comprehensive dataset of global shipping rates, comprising up to 1.5 billion data points from 2004 to 2019, is utilized to investigate the dynamics of the container shipping industry. A novel methodology for analyzing time series data is introduced, enabling the identification of intricate patterns and relationships within the data. This method is applied to examine the impact of the 2008 financial crisis, the 2009-2010 global economic downturn, the 2014-2016 oil price collapse, the 2019-2020 COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2020-2021 COVID-19 vaccine rollout on shipping rates. By analyzing the data, the study reveals a long-standing container crisis that has persisted for over a decade, with a notable decline in rates in 2021. The study also identifies a significant correlation between shipping rates and COVID-19 cases, with a notable increase in rates following the introduction of COVID-19 vaccines.

This paper presents a comprehensive survey of anomaly detection methods for streaming data, with a focus on the key factors driving the effectiveness of anomaly detection algorithms. We examine the various approaches used to categorize these algorithms, as well as the essential components of a typical anomaly detector, and discuss the challenges associated with algorithm design. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the current state of the art in this field, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of existing algorithms, and identifying areas for future research.

Gliomas are the most prevalent type of brain tumor, with the most effective treatment being a combination of surgery and radiation therapy. To support these procedures, researchers have developed a method to segment gliomas into distinct subregions, including the tumor core, enhancing part, and surrounding edema. However, existing segmentation methods often struggle to accurately identify these areas, particularly when dealing with irregularly shaped tumors. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a new approach that utilizes a unique combination of two techniques: a graph-based method to identify and segment enhancing tumors, and a 3D U-Net network to segment edema and tumor core areas. The proposed approach was tested on a large dataset of glioma cases, and the results showed that it outperformed existing methods in accurately identifying and segmenting tumors, edema, and enhancing areas.
